questions.q: a) Define 'Group' in the context of organizational behavior. [2 Marks]
questions.a: A group is two or more individuals who interact and are interdependent in order to achieve a common purpose or goal. Members perceive themselves as part of the group, share certain norms and values, and have a stable pattern of interaction over time. In OB, groups are the building blocks of organizations and may be formal (created by management) or informal (formed naturally). The essential features are regular interaction, a shared identity, common goals and some degree of interdependence. A mere collection of people in the same place, such as a crowd at a bus stop, is not a true group because it lacks structure and continuing interaction.
questions.explanation: This is the standard Robbins-style definition: it names interaction, interdependence, common goal, shared norms and continued interaction as the defining features, and distinguishes a real group from a simple aggregate of people.
questions.oneShotPreview: Group = 2+ people who interact, are interdependent and share a common goal, norms and identity over time.

questions.q: b) Define 'Group Dynamics'. [2 Marks]
questions.a: Group dynamics refers to the interactions, forces and processes that operate among members of a group and that shape its behaviour, structure and performance over time. It is the study of how groups form, develop, communicate, make decisions, establish norms, build cohesiveness and handle conflict. The term emphasizes that a group is a living social system in which the behaviour of the whole is more than the sum of the individual members' behaviour. Understanding group dynamics helps managers predict group behaviour, improve teamwork and make groups more effective. It covers both internal processes (roles, norms, cohesion, decision making) and the external conditions that influence the group.
questions.explanation: This defines the field as the study of interactional forces and processes, stresses the 'whole greater than the sum of parts' idea, and lists the core processes examined in this unit.
questions.oneShotPreview: Group dynamics = study of interactional forces/processes (roles, norms, cohesion, decisions, conflict) shaping group behaviour and performance.

questions.q: c) Define 'Group Behaviour'. [2 Marks]
questions.a: Group behaviour is the pattern of conduct and interaction that emerges when two or more people work together as a group, shaped by the group's structure, processes and the influence members exert on one another. It includes how members communicate, conform to norms, exercise leadership, cooperate or compete, make decisions and respond to pressures such as conflict and outside expectations. Group behaviour differs from individual behaviour because of interdependence, social influence and shared identity. It is affected by factors such as group size, composition, leadership, norms and cohesiveness. Managers study group behaviour to predict performance, reduce dysfunctional conflict and design effective teams.
questions.explanation: This clarifies how group behaviour differs from individual behaviour and links it to the determinants and outcomes covered in the unit.
questions.oneShotPreview: Group behaviour = emergent conduct of members interacting under social influence, shaped by size, composition, leadership, norms and cohesion.

questions.q: Explain the meaning, nature and scope of group dynamics. [5 Marks]
questions.a: Group dynamics means the study of the forces and processes that operate within and between groups and that influence how a group forms, functions and performs. Its nature is interdisciplinary, drawing on psychology and sociology, and it views the group as a dynamic social system in which members continuously influence one another; the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. Its scope covers group formation and development, types of groups, roles and status, norms, cohesiveness, communication, leadership, decision making, conflict and team building. It also examines external conditions such as organizational structure, rewards and the physical environment that affect the group. By applying this knowledge, managers can diagnose group problems, improve cooperation, reduce dysfunctional conflict and raise overall effectiveness. In short, group dynamics links the individual, group and organizational levels of behaviour.
questions.explanation: A 5-mark answer should give the meaning, describe its nature (dynamic, interdisciplinary, systems view), list the topics in its scope and state its managerial purpose.
questions.oneShotPreview: Meaning: forces/processes in groups. Nature: dynamic social system, whole > sum, interdisciplinary. Scope: formation, roles, norms, cohesion, decisions, conflict, team building.

questions.q: a) What is a formal group? [2 Marks]
questions.a: A formal group is a group deliberately created by management to accomplish specific organizational tasks and goals. It has a defined structure with assigned roles, a formal hierarchy, designated leadership and established rules and procedures. Examples include a department, a committee, a project team and a quality circle. Formal groups are also called official or command groups, and their activities are directed toward the organization's objectives. Because roles are officially defined, members have clear expectations about who reports to whom and what each position should do.
questions.explanation: This captures the deliberate, goal-directed, structured nature of formal groups with examples, distinguishing them from naturally formed groups.
questions.oneShotPreview: Formal group = management-created, task-oriented group with defined roles, hierarchy and rules (e.g., department, committee).

questions.q: b) What is an informal group? [2 Marks]
questions.a: An informal group is a group that forms naturally and spontaneously from the social interactions and common interests of employees, without being created or officially recognized by management. It has no formal structure or written rules; instead it develops its own informal norms, roles and a natural leader. Examples include a group of colleagues who lunch together or friends who share a common hobby. Informal groups satisfy members' social needs for friendship, belonging and security and can strongly influence attitudes and work behaviour. They may either support or resist management goals, which is why managers try to understand and work with them.
questions.explanation: This highlights natural formation, absence of official structure, satisfaction of social needs and influence on behaviour - the standard contrast with formal groups.
questions.oneShotPreview: Informal group = naturally formed, unofficial group based on friendship/common interests; no formal structure; meets social needs, influences behaviour.

questions.q: Discuss the various types of groups found in organizations. [10 Marks]
questions.a: Groups in organizations can be classified in several ways. The most basic distinction is between formal groups, created by management to achieve organizational goals (such as departments and task forces), and informal groups, which emerge spontaneously from social interaction to satisfy members' needs for friendship and belonging. Formal groups are further divided into command groups, made up of a manager and the subordinates who report to him or her, and task groups, made up of people working together on a common task, which may cut across normal reporting lines. Robbins also distinguishes task groups (working on tasks) from social groups (formed for fellowship). Another classification is primary groups, characterized by close, face-to-face, lasting relationships and strong emotional ties (such as a family or a small work team), and secondary groups, which are larger, more impersonal and formally organized. Members may also form in-groups, with which a person identifies and feels loyalty, and out-groups, toward which they feel distance or opposition. Other useful categories include friendship groups, interest groups and reference groups, whose norms and values individuals use as a standard for comparing themselves. Each type differs in purpose, structure, durability and influence on the individual and the organization, and managers need to recognize both the formal and the informal side of the group structure in order to work effectively.
questions.explanation: A 10-mark essay should enumerate the main classifications, define each with examples and note why the distinctions matter to managers.
questions.oneShotPreview: Types: formal vs informal; command vs task; task vs social; primary vs secondary; in-group vs out-group; friendship/interest/reference groups.

questions.q: a) What are the determinants of group behaviour? [2 Marks]
questions.a: Determinants of group behaviour are the factors that shape how a group and its members act; they include group size, group composition, leadership, norms, cohesiveness, communication and the external environment. Individual factors such as member personality, ability and attitudes also affect the group, as do organizational factors such as rewards, structure and rules. Together these variables determine the group's interaction patterns, level of cooperation and ultimate performance.
questions.explanation: This gives the standard list of internal, member-level and external determinants in compact form.
questions.oneShotPreview: Determinants: size, composition, leadership, norms, cohesiveness, communication, member traits and external organizational conditions.

questions.q: Explain the various determinants of group behaviour. [5 Marks]
questions.a: Group behaviour is shaped by a combination of internal, member and external factors. Group size matters: small groups allow more interaction and faster agreement, while large groups bring more resources but also more coordination problems, social loafing and subgroup formation. Group composition, especially the diversity of members in ability, personality and background, affects creativity and conflict; heterogeneous groups often generate more ideas but may take longer to cohere. Leadership style strongly influences communication, motivation and decision making. Norms set the standards of acceptable conduct and create conformity pressure, while cohesiveness determines how strongly members are attracted to the group and willing to work together. Communication networks affect the speed and accuracy of information flow, and external conditions such as organizational structure, reward systems, physical layout and task characteristics place further constraints on the group. Individual members bring their own personality, attitudes and abilities, which interact with these group-level forces. Managers can use these determinants to diagnose and improve group functioning.
questions.explanation: A 5-mark answer should name each determinant and briefly explain how it influences group behaviour, ending with the managerial implication.
questions.oneShotPreview: Key determinants: size, composition/diversity, leadership, norms, cohesion, communication networks, member traits, external structure/rewards/task.

questions.q: a) What is group process? [2 Marks]
questions.a: Group process refers to the sequence of interactions and activities through which group members exchange information, coordinate their work and move toward their goals. It includes communication, role differentiation, norm formation, decision making, leadership, conflict management and the stages of group development. Group processes describe how the group works internally rather than what it produces, and they strongly influence the group's effectiveness and member satisfaction.
questions.explanation: This distinguishes process (how members interact) from outcome and lists the principal process activities.
questions.oneShotPreview: Group process = how members interact to work: communication, roles, norms, decisions, leadership, conflict and development stages.

questions.q: Explain the stages of group development proposed by Tuckman. [10 Marks]
questions.a: Bruce Tuckman's model describes five stages that most groups pass through as they develop. In the forming stage, members meet, learn about one another, test relationships and depend heavily on the leader for direction; politeness and uncertainty are common. In the storming stage, conflict and disagreement emerge as members push against authority, compete for roles and express differing ideas; this is a necessary stage for resolving differences. In the norming stage, members develop a shared understanding, establish norms and roles, build cohesiveness and begin to cooperate effectively. In the performing stage, the group is mature and functional: members work interdependently, communicate openly, solve problems and focus on achieving goals, with the leader playing a more delegating role. Tuckman later added a fifth stage, adjourning, for temporary groups, in which members disband after completing the task, with feelings of accomplishment or loss. Groups may regress to earlier stages when membership or tasks change, and the stages vary in length. Understanding the model helps managers recognize that conflict in the storming stage is normal and give the group the right support at each stage.
questions.explanation: A 10-mark essay should name and describe all five stages in sequence, note that adjourning was added later, mention regression and state the managerial relevance.
questions.oneShotPreview: Tuckman: Forming (polite, dependent) -> Storming (conflict) -> Norming (norms, cohesion) -> Performing (effective work) -> Adjourning (disband).

questions.q: a) What are group norms? [2 Marks]
questions.a: Group norms are the shared standards, rules and expectations of behaviour that group members accept as proper and use to guide and evaluate their own and others' conduct. They define what is acceptable, such as how much effort to put in, how to dress, how to communicate and how to treat the leader. Norms develop informally through interaction, are enforced by group pressure and create conformity among members. They may support organizational goals or, in some cases, restrict output and resist management.
questions.explanation: This captures norms as shared standards of acceptable behaviour, how they arise and are enforced, and their double-edged effect on performance.
questions.oneShotPreview: Group norms = shared, often unwritten standards of acceptable behaviour enforced by group pressure; guide and evaluate conduct.

questions.q: Explain how group norms develop and discuss their functions. [5 Marks]
questions.a: Group norms usually develop gradually as members interact and discover which behaviours are accepted; they often begin with a critical event or a suggestion by a respected member and are reinforced as others conform. Key influences include the behaviour of the leader, the group's history, cultural values and the rewards and punishments the group applies. Norms serve several functions: they regulate and predict member behaviour, reduce uncertainty by setting expectations, coordinate effort, express the group's identity and values, protect the group from outside interference and give members a sense of belonging. At the same time, norms create pressure to conform, and this pressure can become strong enough to suppress dissent and lead to poor decisions such as groupthink. Norms are enforced through sanctions ranging from approval and acceptance to criticism or rejection. Managers should therefore shape norms early, since changing established norms is difficult, and ensure that they support rather than undermine organizational goals.
questions.explanation: A 5-mark answer should explain how norms emerge, list their main functions and note both benefits and risks with a managerial implication.
questions.oneShotPreview: Norms develop via interaction/leader example; functions: regulate behaviour, reduce uncertainty, coordinate, express identity, enforce via sanctions; risk: conformity/groupthink.

questions.q: a) Define group cohesiveness. [2 Marks]
questions.a: Group cohesiveness is the degree to which members are attracted to the group, committed to its goals and motivated to remain in it; it is often described as the 'glue' that holds a group together. It shows itself in members' liking for one another, their willingness to cooperate, their sense of shared identity and their resistance to leaving or to outside criticism. Highly cohesive groups interact more frequently, communicate more openly and show higher member satisfaction. Cohesiveness is a key group variable because it influences both how well members work together and how strongly they conform to group norms.
questions.explanation: This defines cohesion as attraction and commitment, names its visible signs and links it to interaction, satisfaction and conformity.
questions.oneShotPreview: Cohesiveness = attraction/commitment binding members to the group ('glue'); shown by liking, cooperation, shared identity and reluctance to leave.

questions.q: Discuss the factors affecting group cohesiveness and its consequences. [10 Marks]
questions.a: Group cohesiveness is the extent to which members are attracted to one another and committed to the group's goals. Several factors increase it: small group size, since fewer members make interaction and agreement easier; similarity of members in attitudes, values and background; frequent and close interaction and shared time together; a clear common goal and shared successes; effective leadership and democratic participation; and external pressure or competition, which makes members close ranks. Hard-to-join groups and groups with a strong identity also tend to be more cohesive. The consequences of cohesiveness are generally positive for morale: members communicate more, cooperate more, help one another and report higher satisfaction, which often improves performance when the group's norms support high output. However, cohesiveness can have negative effects: a highly cohesive group may pressure members to conform, resist change, develop an 'us versus them' attitude and suppress dissent, which can produce groupthink and poor decisions. Cohesiveness and performance are therefore related but not identical, and the effect depends on whether group norms are aligned with organizational goals. Managers should build cohesion through shared goals, participation and recognition while guarding against excessive conformity.
questions.explanation: A 10-mark essay should define cohesiveness, list the factors that build it, discuss both positive and negative consequences and state the managerial implication.
questions.oneShotPreview: Cohesiveness rises with small size, similarity, interaction, shared goals/success, good leadership and external threat; boosts cooperation/satisfaction but risks conformity and groupthink.

questions.q: a) What is a small group? [2 Marks]
questions.a: A small group is a group of relatively few members, usually two to about a dozen, who interact frequently on a personal, face-to-face basis and are strongly interdependent. Because of its size, every member can participate, communicate directly with all others and have a distinct role, which creates close relationships, strong norms and high cohesiveness. Small groups are common in organizations, for example a work team, a committee or a project group, and they are the setting in which most group dynamics such as role formation, norm setting and decision making are studied. Their advantages are quick decisions, flexibility and high member involvement, while disadvantages include a limited range of skills and vulnerability to personality conflicts.
questions.explanation: This gives the size range, the face-to-face and interdependent nature, and notes the advantages and limitations of small groups.
questions.oneShotPreview: Small group = few members (2-12) interacting face-to-face; high participation, strong norms/cohesion; quick decisions but limited resources.

questions.q: a) What is group decision making? b) What is groupthink? [2 Marks]
questions.a: Group decision making is the process by which two or more members jointly analyze a problem, generate alternatives and choose a course of action, as in a committee or team. Compared with individual decisions, groups bring more information and diverse perspectives and tend to produce higher-quality, more acceptable solutions, though the process takes more time and can be dominated by a few members. Groupthink, a concept developed by Irving Janis, is the tendency of a cohesive group to pressure members toward agreement and to suppress dissenting or unusual viewpoints, so that the group values unanimity over a realistic appraisal of alternatives. Its symptoms include an illusion of invulnerability, self-censorship, pressure on dissenters and a belief in the group's inherent morality. The two terms are linked because groupthink is a pressure that can corrupt an otherwise sound group decision-making process.
questions.explanation: This defines both terms clearly and links them: group decision making is the process, while groupthink is a conformity pressure that can distort that process.
questions.oneShotPreview: Group decision making = joint problem solving (more info, slower). Groupthink = cohesion-driven conformity suppressing dissent (Janis).

questions.q: Discuss group decision making, its advantages and limitations, and the techniques that improve it. [10 Marks]
questions.a: Group decision making is the process by which a group jointly identifies a problem, generates alternatives and selects a solution. Its main advantages are that groups bring a wider range of information, knowledge and perspectives, produce more complete and creative alternatives, and generate decisions that members are more likely to accept and implement because they took part. Its limitations are that the process is slower and more costly, can be dominated by one or a few vocal members, creates pressure to conform, may result in compromise rather than the best solution, and diffuses responsibility for the outcome. A major danger is groupthink, described by Irving Janis, in which a highly cohesive group, often under stress and with an insistent leader, values unanimity above critical evaluation; members self-censor, dissent is pressured out, and symptoms such as an illusion of invulnerability and a belief in inherent morality lead to poor decisions. A related problem is groupshift, where group discussion moves members toward more extreme positions. To improve decisions, managers can use brainstorming, where members freely generate ideas without criticism; the nominal group technique, where individuals write ideas independently before group discussion and voting; the Delphi technique, which gathers anonymous judgments from experts through repeated questionnaires; and electronic meetings, which allow simultaneous, anonymous input. Good practice also includes encouraging dissent, appointing a 'devil's advocate', using outside experts and having the leader withhold an early position. Used appropriately, these methods retain the benefits of group input while reducing conformity and process losses.
questions.explanation: A 10-mark essay should define group decision making, weigh advantages against limitations, explain groupthink (and groupshift) and describe the main techniques and safeguards.
questions.oneShotPreview: Group decisions: +info, +acceptance; -slow, conformity, domination. Groupthink = suppressed dissent. Techniques: brainstorming, nominal group, Delphi, electronic meetings, devil's advocate.

questions.q: Explain team building and the different team roles. [5 Marks]
questions.a: Team building is the planned effort to help a group of people develop into an effective, cohesive team by improving communication, trust, cooperation and role clarity. It typically involves activities such as goal setting, role clarification, problem-solving exercises, interpersonal training and sometimes outdoor or experiential tasks. A useful framework is Belbin's team roles, which identifies complementary contributions such as the coordinator who leads and clarifies goals, the shaper who drives the team forward, the plant who generates creative ideas, the monitor-evaluator who judges options, the implementer who turns plans into action, the completer-finisher who ensures accuracy and deadlines, the resource investigator who explores outside contacts, the team worker who supports others and the specialist who provides deep expertise. Effective teams contain a balanced mix of these roles, and members often fill more than one. Team building improves cohesion, reduces misunderstanding and conflict, and raises performance by ensuring that the right behaviours are present. Managers should match roles to members' strengths and continually reinforce shared goals and trust.
questions.explanation: A 5-mark answer should define team building, mention typical activities, outline Belbin's roles and note the benefits and managerial implication.
questions.oneShotPreview: Team building = planned activities to improve trust, roles and cooperation; Belbin roles: coordinator, shaper, plant, monitor, implementer, finisher, investigator, worker, specialist.

questions.q: Discuss conflict in organizations and the styles of conflict resolution. [10 Marks]
questions.a: Organizational conflict is the process that begins when one party perceives that another has negatively affected, or is about to negatively affect, something the first party cares about. It is a normal and inevitable feature of organizational life because people with different goals, values, personalities and interests must work interdependently. Its main sources include task interdependence, competition for scarce resources, unclear roles and responsibilities, communication breakdowns, personality clashes, differing values, power and status differences, and poorly designed reward systems. Conflict is commonly classified as task conflict (disagreement about the content or goals of the work), relationship conflict (interpersonal friction, dislike and animosity) and process conflict (disagreement about how the work should be done). Conflict is not always harmful: moderate task conflict can stimulate ideas, improve decisions and prompt constructive change, making it functional; too much conflict, especially relationship conflict, is dysfunctional and damages morale and performance. The Thomas-Kilmann model describes five resolution styles based on two dimensions, assertiveness and cooperativeness: competing (high assertiveness, low cooperativeness) pursues one's own goals at the other's expense; collaborating (high on both) seeks a win-win solution that fully satisfies both parties; compromising (moderate on both) seeks a middle-ground, mutually acceptable settlement; avoiding (low on both) withdraws or postpones the issue; and accommodating (low assertiveness, high cooperativeness) places the other party's concerns above one's own. Other practical techniques include problem solving or confrontation, in which parties face the issue and find a genuine solution, and negotiation. No single style is best: the appropriate choice depends on the importance of the issue, the relationship, the time available and the power balance. Managers should encourage functional task conflict, prevent it from turning into personal hostility, and select the resolution style that fits the situation.
questions.explanation: A 10-mark essay should define conflict, give its sources and types (task/relationship/process), distinguish functional from dysfunctional conflict, present all five Thomas-Kilmann styles on the assertiveness-cooperativeness axes and state when each is appropriate.
questions.oneShotPreview: Conflict = perceived threat to one's interests; sources: resources, roles, communication, personality. Types: task/relationship/process. T-K styles: competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, accommodating.
